question: Is goodness born in people, as Mencius held, or made by training, as Xunzi held?
answer: Anyone who sees a toddler about to fall into a well feels alarm and pity, Mencius argued, before any thought of reward or reputation: goodness has sprouts that need only tending. Modern studies partly agree. In 2006, 18-month-olds picked up objects an adult had dropped and could not reach, unasked and unrewarded, again and again.
move: It turns on whether early kindness or early violence better reveals human nature.
counterpoint: Human nature is bad, Xunzi wrote; goodness comes from deliberate effort, as warped wood is straightened by steaming and pressing. Children bear him out too: Richard Tremblay's studies of Quebec children found hitting, biting and kicking most frequent in toddlerhood, declining as children are taught otherwise. Nobody has to teach a toddler to hit.
reference: Hutton (trans.), Xunzi: The Complete Text, Princeton University Press, 2014; Warneken & Tomasello, Altruistic helping in human infants and young chimpanzees, Science 311, 2006; Tremblay et al., Physical aggression during early childhood, Pediatrics 114, 2004
